newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin comes back amid political storm - his own.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin comes back amid political storm - his own.

text.p: It is small wonder that President Boris Yeltsin returns to the helm in the very eye of a political storm and that black clouds are seen to swirl over so many of those around him.

It is no surprise because Yeltsin, reasserting his authority after long illness, himself unleashed the tempest. Such is his trademark style, cutting everyone down to size to maintain an unchallenged grip on power.
Russia's ruling elite and the media it influences have been buffeted by speculation this week over who is, or is not, about to be sacked. The conclusions vary enormously, as is Yeltsin's calculation.
Yet, after a rumble of in-fighting last summer when Yeltsin first announced he needed heart surgery, they were all curiously united while the president's ability to rule hung in the balance.

Even communist leaders, now effectively part of the elite through their dominance in parliament and a number of top regional government jobs, sounded faint-hearted in their own demands Yeltsin step down on health grounds.
The reason for this consensus, at least beneath the surface of daily politics, appears to be that an early election could well put General Alexander Lebed into the Kremlin.
Yeltsin's popular former security adviser is not part of the "system", he does not play by the rules and this has scared Establishment circles, forcing them to bury their differences.
Lebed may not appear to have a coherent economic programme or a stable team of advisers and backers. But he seemed bound to try to fulfil promises to crush corruption and restore order.

Those already sharing power in Yeltsin's post-Soviet order realised Lebed would not only launch his own personnel reshuffle but also start redistributing spheres of influence and -- much more important than jobs -- Russia's prime economic assets.
Media loyal to the Kremlin, especially powerful television channels, played down Yeltsin's health troubles, rallied behind Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and targeted Lebed.
Differences between Chernomyrdin, Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais and high-flying Moscow mayor Yuri Luzhkov seemed temporarily forgotten in the face of the Lebed threat.
Some liberals even started talking about a secret deal between Chernomyrdin and senior communists in parliament.

"We are seeing an advanced state of unity in the political regime formed after 1993," wrote analyst Lidiya Shevtsova in the liberal daily Nezavisimaya Gazeta. In 1993 Yeltsin crushed the Soviet-era parliament with military force and won vast new constitutional powers.
"A stable practice has been worked out where...cooperation mechanisms between major influence groups have been formed... and opposition has became an element of the establishment."
But, the moment -- some time in late February -- when it became clear that Yeltsin, albeit still physically weak, was firmly back in power, a political storm broke out.
And it was the president himself who unleashed it.

He warned the communist-dominated parliament he was ready to fight it -- raising memories of the bloodshed of 1993. And he told Chernomyrdin he had to reshuffle the cabinet -- both comments in full view of the cameras on Sunday and Monday.

Yeltsin chose his words carefully. With his celebrated political intuition, he realised that social discontent over unpaid wages and pensions and dying industries was reaching a point when it threatened his own authority, eight months into a second term.
The comeback president needs high-profile scapegoats and his fire seems directed at ministers in charge of the economy.
In a radio address on Friday he blasted the 1997 budget, calling it "bad" and "unrealistic" and saying he would take more personal charge of government financial affairs in future.
He added fuel to the flames by rebuking Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, telling him not to "whine" and reform the army.

No Kremlin leader can afford a disgruntled army for long and Yeltsin knows that. He must recall the debt he owes the military for their reluctant decision to back him and pound communist and nationalist rebels into submission in the White House parliament in 1993.
Politicians and the media took the bait on Yeltsin's remarks.
Rodionov will be out, many of them speculated this week.

Some also say Chernomyrdin's days are numbered, others say Yeltsin cannot afford to dump his most loyal ally of the last four years and his only aim is to cut down to size a premier who effectively ran the country while Yeltsin was ill.

Nearly every minister has been mentioned somewhere in the media as facing the axe. The climax is expected on March 6, when Yeltsin delivers his annual state of the nation address to parliament and the cabinet reviews the results of the past year.

"Everyone thinks Yeltsin will mark his return by big changes because the time has come for them. But no one knows exactly what he will do," said Sergei Parkhomenko, editor of the influential liberal news weekly Itogi. "That's why everyone is trying to distance himself from everyone else. Just in case..."
